title: Research-scale machine-checked mathematical discovery

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a system that creates new research-level mathematical arguments across several mainstream subjects and produces machine-checkable proofs of its conclusions. A human supplies a research goal in ordinary mathematical language, while the system develops the argument without a human proof sketch. Its work would include translating the goal faithfully into a formal statement, finding useful intermediate results, and assembling a proof that a proof assistant can check. This is the proposed capability, whose achievement is not established by the supplied evidence.

Lean provides a foundation for checking generated proof terms. The assurance applies to the formal statement and its declared axioms, subject to the soundness of the checking machinery. Faithful translation remains a separate requirement. The AlphaProof paper describes training on automatically formalized problems even when their correspondence to the original natural-language statements is imperfect. A valid proof of such a formal problem therefore leaves the fidelity of the translation to be established.

The intended scope extends across research problems that require sustained argument and the development of useful mathematical concepts. The AlphaProof paper identifies extension to research mathematics and theory building as a substantial next step. For this record, the target is an explicitly bounded, useful range of research tasks, with breadth demonstrated through evaluation.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment. A system that reliably turns stated research goals into faithful, kernel-checked proofs or disproofs, at a cost comparable to a human research project, would introduce a major new means of producing mathematics. New checked research theorems would follow directly from that capability. The supplied paper documents substantial expert labour in existing formalization successes and substantial computation in its competition-proof system, providing concrete context for the proposed advance.

Interpretive synthesis. The comparison with inexpensive steel expresses a possible change in the production of mathematics, as a foundational input becomes easier to produce and use. Its force depends on reliability, cost, breadth, and accessibility. The analogy supplies no quantitative prediction about the scale or timing of the effect. The proposed cost comparison with human research also remains an evaluation objective, without an established economic measurement in the supplied material.

Routine auditing of papers would require the system to recover intended statements, assumptions, and argument structure faithfully. The paper's distinction between a formally valid training problem and a faithful translation explains why proof checking alone cannot supply that assurance. Broad paper auditing would consequently be an additional capability to demonstrate.

Downstream synthesis. Dependable mathematical libraries could benefit from automated proof construction and repeated checking, while still requiring maintenance of definitions, dependencies, toolchains, and correspondence with intended mathematics. Software verification could also benefit from stronger mathematical automation, with specifications continuing to determine the properties being verified. These possibilities depend on additional integration and maintenance capabilities.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in the proposal is autonomous research-level argument creation across multiple subjects, combined with trustworthy formal verification and faithful interpretation of human goals. The supplied AlphaProof paper documents technical foundations and research-extension challenges. It leaves the field-wide availability of the proposed capability as of 1 November 2026 unresolved.

Proof search must discover productive intermediate steps and adapt to difficult goals within workable resource budgets. Informal-to-formal translation must preserve quantifiers, hypotheses, definitions, and the intended conclusion. Library coverage must provide the concepts and results needed to express and solve the problem. The AlphaProof evaluation relied on experts to formalize competition statements, illustrating a material human contribution that a goal-only system would have to absorb.

Research mathematics also requires theory building, including the introduction of concepts and the continuous expansion of the available library. The paper explicitly identifies this transition as challenging. A system would need to generate definitions and auxiliary results that support further reasoning while preserving a checkable dependency structure.

Engineering synthesis. Long research arguments would require coordination of intermediate claims, dependencies, and revisions over extended searches. Their length is a plausible scaling concern retained from the research input, although the supplied review identifies no passage independently establishing it as a measured barrier. Practical progress would require evidence about reliability and resource use as argument size and conceptual depth increase.

current_state.text: In the documented 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad evaluation, AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 together solved four of six problems and scored 28 out of 42 points, equivalent to silver-medal level. AlphaProof solved P1, P2, and P6, accounting for three of the five non-geometry problems. AlphaGeometry 2 solved the geometry problem P4. These are dated competition results reported in the Nature paper, published on 12 November 2025.

Experts manually formalized all five non-geometry problem statements in Lean after their release. Each of AlphaProof's three successful solutions required 2–3 days of test-time reinforcement learning. This establishes multi-day problem-specific adaptation and a substantial human role in statement preparation. The paper places its successes primarily within advanced high-school and undergraduate competition mathematics and describes extension to research mathematics as a considerable next step.

The research input mentions reports from September and October 2026 of large Lean formalizations of existing theorems, including a claimed formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem. No supplied evidence documents those reports or establishes the completeness of the claimed formalizations. Their existence, scope, and completion remain unverified within this record. Successful formalization of an existing proof would demonstrate the scale of formal checking and formalization, while autonomous discovery requires evidence of newly created research arguments.

The evidence review relied on retained article and Methods prose from the identified Nature paper. It described the reviewed representation as partial because figure images and some table contents were unavailable. The numerical evaluation results above are supported by the retained prose. Although the source index lists saved HTML, paper PDF, and supplementary PDF artifacts without recorded extraction issues, those listings do not establish that every artifact or visual element received substantive review.

The supplied freshness search record is empty, so it does not establish the field's state on 1 November 2026 or resolve developments after the documented evaluation. This leaves the current availability of the full proposed capability open. The dated 2024 results retain their evidential support.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Evaluate the system on a blinded set of previously unpublished research problems from at least four areas, such as algebra, analysis, combinatorics, and number theory. It should produce kernel-checked proofs that independent specialists accept as research contributions, including at least one result settling a previously open question. Human participation should be limited to stating the goals. Four areas is a proposed breadth threshold chosen for this record.
completion_criteria.label: Kernel-checked research contributions across four areas, settling an open question

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol. Define blinding, problem provenance, novelty checks, permitted human intervention, accepted axioms, library versions, and resource budgets before evaluation. Independently assess whether each formal statement faithfully expresses the submitted goal. Record every clarification and intervention so that the claimed autonomy can be evaluated. For a disproof, require a checked derivation or a formally verified counterexample sufficient to refute the intended statement.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined evaluation protocol verifies goal fidelity and records human intervention

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements. Release proof artifacts, formal statements, declared axioms, dependency versions, and instructions sufficient for independent checking. Report search time, computational resources, failures, and human labour alongside successful results. Independent groups should reproduce the checks, and repeated blinded evaluations should establish how consistently the system discovers acceptable research arguments.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible proof artifacts and repeated blinded evaluations with full accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries. Report the subjects, problem types, library prerequisites, costs, and levels of conceptual novelty covered by the demonstrations. Competition performance and formalization of known proofs can provide supporting evidence for particular components. The research-discovery demonstration additionally requires novelty, faithful goal interpretation, and goal-only human input. Any finite evaluation establishes breadth on the tested problems and conditions, with generalization remaining an empirical question.
completion_criteria.label: Reported practical boundaries constrain claims to tested problems and conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. MAT-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, overlaps through algorithm discovery and complexity proofs. MAT-05 could help formulate or verify such arguments. Establishing MAT-01 would require the specific algorithms, correctness guarantees, and practical complexity properties associated with that entry. Research-proof automation alone supplies no such guarantee.

Roster-based synthesis. MAT-02, An effective global Langlands correspondence over number fields, presents a possible domain for research-level discovery and theory building. MAT-05 concerns a general capability for creating checked mathematics, while MAT-02 concerns a particular mathematical correspondence and its effective realization. Progress on either could support the other through new results and formal libraries.

Roster-based synthesis. MAT-03, A first-principles theory of turbulent transport, and MAT-04, Proved polynomial-cost solution of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs, could draw on automated derivation and verification of mathematical results. MAT-03 would also require establishing the physical relevance of its theory. MAT-04 would require the stated algorithmic cost and solution guarantees. A checked proof certifies consequences of formal assumptions, leaving model adequacy and the applicability of those assumptions to be established.

Roster-based synthesis. MAT-06, Classical polynomial-time integer factorization and discrete logarithms, and MAT-09, Classical polynomial-time algorithms for cryptographic lattice problems, overlap with MAT-05 through the possible discovery and checking of algorithms and complexity proofs. Each retains its own problem-specific performance requirements. A broadly capable mathematical discovery system might contribute to those goals, with success requiring separate demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis. MAT-07, A prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning, could inform the design of mathematical reasoning systems and could itself receive contributions from automated theorem discovery. Its target is a theory that guides deep-learning practice. MAT-05 targets the production of new checked mathematical arguments across subjects.

Roster-based synthesis. MAT-08, Polynomial-time chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure, could benefit from checked derivations and algorithmic error bounds. Its completion would require the specified computational scaling and chemical accuracy across its intended domain. Mathematical discovery automation could assist with those requirements, whose achievement would need independent evidence.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system had achieved the full proposed capability by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The existence, scope, completeness, and checking status of the reported September–October 2026 formalizations, including the Fermat's Last Theorem claim, remain unverified.
No supplied measurement establishes the proposed system's cost relative to a human research project or the magnitude of its potential economic impact.
A future evaluation must operationalize research novelty, blinding, goal-only human participation, accepted axioms, resource budgets, and faithful translation.
The role of research-argument length as a scaling barrier remains a reasoned engineering concern without specific supporting evidence in the supplied review.
The source index lists multiple saved artifacts, while the substantive review describes partial access to visual and table content. No broader inspection is inferred from artifact availability.

brief.title: New mathematics with proofs computers can check
possible: A mathematician could state a research question in ordinary mathematical language and receive a new proof or disproof that software checks step by step. The system would develop the argument across several subjects without needing a human proof sketch.
why: Researchers would gain another way to produce mathematical knowledge, with proofs that others could check automatically. Useful intermediate results could become building blocks for further research.

sources.showed: AlphaProof solved difficult competition problems using Lean, software that checks mathematical proofs. Experts translated the questions into Lean, and successful searches took days.
sources.quote: AlphaProof substantially improves state-of-the-art results on historical mathematics competition problems.
sources.cited_for: Competition mathematics demonstrated proof search backed by automatic checking.
sources.not_established: This did not demonstrate autonomous research discovery from questions stated in ordinary mathematical language.

sources.who: Haocheng Ju, Guoxiong Gao, Jiedong Jiang and collaborators
sources.showed: This preprint reports resolving an open algebra problem and producing a Lean proof with essentially no human involvement.
sources.quote:

demonstrate that strong theorem retrieval tools enable the discovery and application of deep, cross-domain
mathematical techniques, while the formal agent is capable of autonomously filling nontrivial gaps in
informal arguments.
sources.cited_for: It connects research problem solving with automatically checked proofs.
sources.not_established: The case studies do not establish reliable discovery across subjects under independent, blinded evaluation.

sources.who: George Tsoukalas and collaborators at Google DeepMind, Aarhus University and Google

agent solved all 9 problems, though at a higher cost on the harder problems.

sources.not_established: The system starts with a human-prepared Lean statement rather than translating an ordinary-language goal itself.

Our formalization is complete, contains no unproven placeholders (sorry), and uses only the standard ax‑
ioms of classical mathematics.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates large proof construction and repairs to existing research mathematics.
sources.not_established: Supervised translation of an existing argument does not establish autonomous discovery from a research goal.

shown: Research discovery has moved beyond competition problems in reported preprints. Ju and collaborators report solving an open algebra problem with essentially no human involvement. Google DeepMind and collaborators report checked proofs of open problems, starting from human-prepared Lean statements.

Lu and collaborators report assembling a long checked proof under human supervision. Together, these results demonstrate parts of the capability, while leaving the full combination of independent discovery, faithful translation and breadth to be demonstrated.
missing: A system has yet to demonstrate research discovery across subjects with humans supplying only ordinary-language goals.
Faithful translation and useful new concepts must work together throughout sustained research arguments.
Repeated independent evaluations must establish reliability, failures and total resource use.

milestones.label: Checked research discoveries across four subjects
milestones.explanation: A blinded test would have to yield checked, expert-accepted contributions across four subjects, including a previously open question, from unpublished goals alone. This would establish research discovery and breadth.

milestones.label: Independent checks confirm meaning and human involvement
milestones.explanation: A predefined test would have to check faithful translation, novelty, assumptions, budgets and every human intervention, including checked disproofs. This would establish what the system proved and how independently it worked.

milestones.label: Others reproduce checks and repeat discovery tests
milestones.explanation: Released proofs, statements, assumptions and software dependencies would have to support independent checking, with repeated blinded tests reporting failures, computing and human effort. This would establish consistency and cost.

milestones.label: Practical limits are measured and reported
milestones.explanation: Demonstrations would have to report subjects, problem types, required mathematical libraries, costs and conceptual novelty. This would keep claims tied to tested conditions and distinguish discovery from reproducing known proofs.

uncertain: It remains unclear how reliably systems can invent useful concepts when existing mathematical libraries are insufficient.
The cost relative to a human research project remains unmeasured.
Research novelty, faithful translation and acceptable human help still need clear evaluation rules.

page.title: Autonomous mathematical discovery with formal proofs
page.definition: A system develops new research-level proofs or disproofs in multiple mathematical subjects from ordinary-language questions alone. It translates each question faithfully and supplies proofs accepted by a proof assistant’s kernel, the program that checks deductions from axioms.

goal.need: At the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad, experts translated all five non-geometry questions into Lean; AlphaProof’s three successful searches each required 2–3 days. Research proof search also retains human checking of statement meaning. Automating these tasks would extend proof checking to the creation of mathematical arguments and their formal statements.

completion.title: An AI settles an open research problem with a formally checked proof and journal acceptance.
completion.criterion: An AI system, starting from an ordinary-language statement and without human proof guidance, settles a previously open research problem with a proof checked in a proof assistant, and at least one such result has been accepted after journal peer review.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; an owner-set completion test, not an adopted field standard.
completion.basis: The entry owner set this bar on November 15, 2026, judging that requiring the same system across several mathematical subjects and separate specialist sign-off exceeded what the goal needs.

milestones.title: An automated prover produces a complete proof accepted by Lean using only its standard axioms.
milestones.criterion: The generated proof passes an independent invocation of Lean on the complete theorem and proof. Its dependencies use only propositional extensionality, choice and quotient soundness. AlphaProof reported satisfying this check for three of the five non-geometry problems from the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad, with human-prepared formal statements.
milestones.set_by: Google DeepMind, AlphaProof Methods, “Proof verification final check”.
milestones.threshold_quote: every proof or disproof found by AlphaProof undergoes a final, independent verification step.

milestones.title: AI agents complete a research-theorem formalization with no open proof obligations.
milestones.criterion: All dependencies compile, statements express the intended mathematics, and every proof obligation is discharged using standard foundational axioms. Human supervision is permitted. FormalFlow reports a proof of quantum soundness for the classical low individual-degree test, with corrected hypotheses: 63 days and 126,367 lines across 337 files. Human experts reviewed the statements and definitions. These are preprint results in version 3, submitted on 21 October 2026, not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Lu et al., FormalFlow’s published completion criterion; demonstrated on a theorem in quantum complexity.
milestones.threshold_quote: all dependencies compile, all statements express the intended mathematics accurately, and no open proof obligations remain.

milestones.title: An AI settles an open formal conjecture with a checked proof of the intended statement.
milestones.criterion: A conjecture without a known solution receives a kernel-accepted proof without forbidden axioms. Manual inspection confirms that the formal statement expresses the intended open problem. Formal Conjectures explicitly requires this fidelity check. AlphaProof Nexus reports passing this test on Erdős problems in its preprint version dated 8 June 2026; the evaluation counts appear in the goal table. The results are not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Formal Conjectures benchmark authors, Section 4.1, “Evaluating Open Problems” and “Correctness”.
milestones.threshold_quote: Solutions are correct if and only if accepted by the kernel without relying on forbidden axioms, such as sorry.

milestones.title: An AI discovers and formalizes an open-problem solution without human proof guidance.
milestones.criterion: A natural-language research question is resolved and its solution fully formalized without human proof guidance. Final validation compares the theorem with a human-reviewed specification and permits only standard Lean axioms. Ju et al. report this for Anderson’s commutative-algebra problem, allowing humans to retrieve inaccessible references: approximately 80 hours of agent runtime and 19,448 lines across 42 files. The preprint was first submitted on 4 April 2026 and is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Ju et al., Sections 4.3–4.4, end-to-end discovery and formalization evaluation; demonstrated for one commutative-algebra problem.
milestones.threshold_quote: the only human intervention consisted of downloading paywalled PDF files that Archon could not retrieve on its own

not_found: No outside body’s numerical requirement for mathematical subject breadth was found.
No published evaluation was located that establishes the combined completion test, including journal acceptance and goal-only input throughout discovery and formalization.
